newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Church leaders condemn "shameful" Australian death.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Church leaders condemn "shameful" Australian death.

text.p: Australian church leaders on Thursday condemned the country's first legally assisted suicide, describing it as a "shameful day for Australia".
Reacting to news that a dying man in the outback Northern Territory had become the first person to use the territory's voluntary euthanasia law, they warned that Australia's moral future was at risk.

"At least this deplorable act may serve to bring the stark reality of euthanasia fully home to the consciousness of all Australians and further instances of this ugly evil may yet be prevented," Sydney's Roman Catholic archbishop, Cardinal Edward Clancy, said in a statement.
Clancy said it was "a shameful day for Australia".

The Anglican Archbishop of Sydney, Harry Goodhew, added: "It has now been shown to us what this means...Doctors are no longer those who save lives, under the Northern Territory law they are also those who kill."
A spokesman for Clancy's Sydney diocese warned that the law threatened those who were vulnerable in society and would tempt doctors to carry out euthanasia on them.
"It puts at risk those who are vulnerable, particularly those suffering dementia," he said. "Then there will be a very strong temptation to use euthanasia on economic grounds."

The Northern Territory law permitting medically assisted suicide under tightly-controlled conditions came into operation on July 1. It has been widely condemned around the world, including by the Vatican, although polls in Australia suggested many citizens support the concept of mercy killing.
A previous attempt by a terminally ill New South Wales taxi-driver to use the law was foiled when the man could not find the doctors needed to approve his death. He has since died.
But Philip Nitschke, a doctor from the Northern Territory capital of Darwin, said on Thursday that he had helped an elderly Darwin cancer patient take his own life on Sunday.
The law is being challenged in both the federal parliament and the Australian High Court.
The death of the unidentified man was greeted with dismay in by Australia's Right to Life organisation.
"I also feel ashamed to be an Australian," said the organisation's chairwoman, Margaret Tighe.
